activities.caption: put the October 2021 collapse in order
activities.name: distOutageOrder

config.prompt: Put the October 2021 collapse in order:
items: Facebook withdraws the BGP announcements that tell the internet how to reach its DNS servers
Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp vanish for about six hours
The company's own staff cannot easily reach the buildings or tools to fix it — internal routes went down with the announcement
Serious teams begin treating routing and DNS as safety-critical
config.why: The distributed-system lesson in one afternoon — the mechanisms everyone reuses are the ones that can take a planet offline.

activities.anchor: Production systems operationalise it with quorums
activities.caption: tune the read and write settings yourself
activities.name: distQuorumBranch

config.root: N = 3 replicas of one shard. Tune the settings.

start.text: Writes need W acknowledgements; reads wait for R responses. Default suggestion?

choices.label: W = 2, R = 2 — W + R = 4 exceeds N
choices.feedback: Every read must overlap at least one fresh copy — consistency survives one crashed node, at the cost of every read contacting two machines.

choices.label: W = 1, R = 1 — fastest
choices.feedback: Writes to one copy leave two stale: a read from a stale node returns old data — fast, and eventually consistent.

fast.text: Stale reads accepted. What does that buy during a cut?

choices.label: Availability — answer from whatever copy you have
choices.feedback: The CAP availability side: the system keeps answering while copies disagree.

choices.label: Consistency — refuse reads that cannot reach a threshold
choices.feedback: The CAP consistency side: no answers during the cut, but nothing wrong leaves the building.

safe.text: The safe setting. What breaks it?

choices.label: A second node crashes — W = 2 now unreachable
choices.feedback: With one live node, writes must refuse: the consistency side of CAP during a cut.

avail.text: Available and eventually consistent — the DNS school: staleness accepted, answers always.

consis.text: Consistent and unavailable during the cut — the bank-balance school: wrong is worse than slow.

down.text: Two down of three: no write threshold can be met, so the store refuses writes — availability sacrificed for consistency, one request at a time.

config.why: Tune W and R per request, per piece of data — the CAP call belongs to the operation, not to the company.

activities.name: distWorkloadSort

config.prompt: File each workload by the mode that suits it:

items.label: refuse reads that cannot reach a threshold

config.why: Engineers who misread the theorem as one-mode-for-everything build systems that are either slow everywhere or wrong where it counts.

activities.anchor: Money is the hardest distributed-systems problem dressed in economics
activities.caption: call the settlement rate
activities.name: distTpsEst

config.prompt: At the protocol's base layer, roughly how many payments can this network settle per second?
config.why: About 7 — Visa peaks in the tens of thousands; and each one burns more energy than many homes use in a year, which is why Ethereum switched its agreement mechanism in 2022.
config.context: Rewriting history means re-mining every block since — economically self-defeating against an honest majority.

activities.anchor: The trade-offs are the distributed-systems trade-offs wearing a currency
activities.caption: drag the divider across the two agreement machines
activities.name: distConsensusCompare

config.prompt: Two ways to buy the Byzantine Generals result — drag the divider:

before.label: proof-of-work
before.text: Miners burn electricity: roughly 10²⁰ hashes per second network-wide, each block about 10 minutes of global luck — consensus bought with energy.

after.label: proof-of-stake
after.text: Validators stake coins instead of burning electricity — Ethereum's 2022 switch cut energy use by an estimated 99.9%.

config.why: Both buy agreement without a referee — and 'immutable' still has an asterisk: a majority cartel can reorganise recent blocks, so the guarantees are economic and probabilistic.

activities.anchor: Distributing machines distributes the attack surface
activities.caption: pair each mechanism with the layer it guards
activities.name: distGuardMatch

config.prompt: Pair each mechanism with the layer it guards:

pairs.right: data on the wire — nothing more
service-to-service calls once attackers are inside — the zero-trust assumption
replay — the network WILL deliver your payment request twice
assaults no single machine could survive

config.why: Mirai, 2016: hundreds of thousands of weak-password IoT devices flooded DNS provider Dyn — Twitter, Netflix and Reddit off the air for hours.

activities.anchor: Underneath replication sits the crown jewel
activities.caption: true or false — the consensus arithmetic
activities.name: distRaftJudge

statements.s: Raft elects one leader and requires a majority to confirm each log entry.
statements.why: 2 of 3, 3 of 5 — the arithmetic IS the safety argument.

statements.s: Paxos is famous for being nearly incomprehensible; Raft re-solved the problem to be teachable.
Two majorities can carry conflicting decisions.
statements.why: Any two majorities overlap in at least one live node — conflicting decisions cannot both carry a majority.

statements.s: etcd stores Kubernetes' entire cluster state on top of this machinery.
statements.why: etcd, CockroachDB, Spanner — agreement with an engine attached.

activities.caption: fill the blanks — why the tails eat the average
activities.name: distTailCloze

config.text: A service that calls %%0%% others, each 99.9% reliable, succeeds fully only about %%1%%% of the time — 1% of a million requests per day is %%2%% failures. A struggling service receiving three retries per failure is under %%3%%× the load it was already failing under.
config.hint: Hedged requests, backpressure and circuit breakers are the tail-taming toolkit.
